subtopic: TensorRT build cost vs runtime cost
learningObjective: Reason about the split between one-time build cost and per-inference runtime cost in TensorRT, and identify a common misdiagnosis when comparing to eager PyTorch.
stem: A team benchmarks their model as follows: 'TensorRT 8 min, PyTorch eager 0.2 s'. What is the most likely source of confusion in this comparison?

options.text: TensorRT is always slower than PyTorch eager for BERT-sized models on modern GPUs; the 0.2 s PyTorch number reflects steady-state kernel launches, whereas TensorRT's kernel selection heuristics never converge to a competitive plan for transformer workloads.
TensorRT's build step must be repeated on every inference call, whereas PyTorch eager amortizes it via warmup, which is why the 8-minute number is a per-call cost that dominates end-to-end latency.

PyTorch eager is missing calls to `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, so the 0.2 s is entirely CPU-side dispatch cost; TensorRT does not require synchronization, so its 8 minutes is a true GPU-side execution time.

The 8 minutes is the TensorRT engine build cost, which is a one-time offline compilation of the model; the correct comparison against PyTorch eager is per-inference latency of the deserialized engine, not build time. Build cost and inference latency should never be added together for the deployment comparison.

explanation: TensorRT's builder can spend minutes or more selecting tactics, calibrating precision and running optimization passes; this is a one-time offline cost. The relevant comparison for deployment is per-inference latency of the deserialized engine (typically milliseconds or less). Conflating build cost with inference cost is a common miscommunication in benchmarks.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: TensorRT commonly outperforms PyTorch eager on transformers.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: build is one-time offline, not per-call.

assumptions: The 8-minute number is the reported TensorRT build time, not an inference latency.
nonImplications: Does not imply build time is irrelevant; long build times matter for iterative development and canary deploys.
Does not imply eager PyTorch is always slower at inference; small models with tiny kernels may favor eager.

distractorRationales.B: Wrong split of one-time vs per-call.
